AN ACT
Amending Title 35 (Health and Safety) of the Pennsylvania
Consolidated Statutes, providing for online gambling public
health and consumer protection; and establishing a restricted
account within the Compulsive and Problem Gambling Treatment
Fund and the Online Problem Gambling Public Health Task
Force.
The General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
hereby enacts as follows:
Section 1. Title 35 of the Pennsylvania Consolidated
Statutes is amended by adding a chapter to read:
CHAPTER 60
ONLINE GAMBLING PUBLIC HEALTH
AND CONSUMER PROTECTION

§ 6001. Scope of chapter.
This chapter relates to online gambling public health and
consumer protection.
§ 6002. Legislative intent.
The General Assembly recognizes the following public policy
purposes and declares that the following objectives of the
Commonwealth are to be served by this chapter:
(1) A major change to Pennsylvania's gambling industry
has been the increased availability of online gambling,
including greater access to Internet and mobile betting
platforms, which has become the fastest method of gambling
for both traditional casino-style gambling and sports
betting.
(2) The smartphone, which is one of the most common ways
for consumers to engage in online gambling, is itself
engineered to encourage frequent and continuous use by
consumers.
(3) Online gambling applications and platforms, and the
online wagers they feature, have been designed to capitalize
on consumer engagement techniques established and employed by
social media applications.
(4) The combination of constant, easy and immediate
access with the advances in smartphone technology and game

and wagering content design has resulted in online gambling
having significant differences from traditional forms of
gambling in physical casinos.
(5) Despite its economic benefits, some experts have
correlated the growth of online gambling to increases in
problem-gambling rates and expressed concerns regarding
minors being exposed to sports betting content.
(6) The Professor of Global Health at Harvard
University's T.H. Chan School of Public Health has said that
online gambling can be 10 times more harmful than other forms
of gambling and that it is continuous, intense and can be
physically, mentally and financially harmful.
(7) According to the University of California Los
Angeles Gambling Studies Program, younger people are at
higher risk of developing gambling disorders than adults and
there is an increase in access to casino-style gambling and
sports betting, with a multitude of online platforms offering
online and mobile betting.
(8) Problem gambling prevalence rates in states with
legal online gambling consistently trend to be among the
highest in the nation, often more than three times the
national average.
(9) Problem gambling may lead to repeated, uncontrolled
gambling that can result in negative consequences to an
individual, leading to the loss of relationships, jobs and
other opportunities. Further, experts contend that each
person who suffers from problem gambling impacts eight other
individuals, whether family members, coworkers or others.
(10) Several studies conducted in states with online
gambling, including Pennsylvania and New Jersey, show that

high risk for problem gambling.
(11) The Pennsylvania Interactive Gaming Assessment:
Online Gambling Report, conducted for the Commonwealth by The
Pennsylvania State University, has revealed the following:
(i) Rates of problem gambling are 4 to 12 times
higher among those that gamble online, with those that
gamble online and offline, such as through the lottery or
brick and mortar casinos, experiencing the highest rates
of problem gambling.
(ii) Online gamblers spend as much as four times the
amount of time gambling as other gamblers and nearly half
of online gamblers report gambling in isolation.
(iii) A growing number of online gamblers report
they are out of work.
(iv) Intake calls to Pennsylvania's 1-800 Helpline
have dramatically increased since the advent of online
gambling in this Commonwealth, with a majority of all
calls to the Helpline being about online gambling.
(v) Ten percent of mixed-modal gamblers, online and
retail, report having in excess of $300,000 in household
debt.
(vi) The problem gambling prevalence rate in
Pennsylvania is as much as four times the national
average and, for mixed-modal gamblers, the rate is 10
times the national average.
(12) A survey by the National Council on Problem
Gambling found that:
(i) An estimated 12,000,000 individuals who are
between 18 and 34 years of age, the first generation to

(ii) A majority of those individuals gamble on debt.
(iii) A large majority of individuals surveyed

(13) The National Bureau of Economic Research found that
the legalization of online sports betting in states across
the country has resulted in an additional 284,000 food-
insufficient households and over $130,000,000 in excess
healthcare expenditures annually.
(14) The Sports Betting and Related Interactive Gambling
in Pennsylvania Study, prepared by the Joint State Government
Commission pursuant to House Resolution 60 of 2025, reported
the following:
(i) According to a 2025 poll of United States
residents, 48% of men between 18 and 49 years of age had
an account with at least one online sportsbook, compared
with 22% of Americans overall.
(ii) Fifty-two percent of respondents reported
betting an increased amount in the hope of recovering
money after a loss, a behavior described as chasing a
bet.
(iii) According to a 2026 poll conducted by The
Harris Poll on behalf of the National Council on Problem
Gambling, 79% of Americans believe gambling addiction is
as serious as, or more serious than, alcohol or drug
addiction.
(iv) Sixty-five percent of adults 21 years of age or
older reported participating in at least one form of

(v) Research using actual player data found that a
small percentage of customers generate a disproportionate
share of gambling revenue and frequently gamble at levels
associated with an elevated risk of gambling-related
harm.
(vi) Studies from the United States and abroad found
that a disproportionate share of gambling revenue is
generated by a relatively small percentage of players. An
analysis by the French gambling regulator found that
problem gamblers represented 8.7% of registered players
but accounted for 60% of total gross gaming revenue.
Similarly, a study using actual player data from legal
United States online gambling operators found that 5.7%
of online sports bettors and 4.9% of online casino
players accounted for 80% of sports betting and online
casino expenditures, respectively.
(vii) The Sports Betting and Related Interactive
Gambling in Pennsylvania Study reported that, during 2019
and 2020, VIP sports bettors at one legal online
sportsbook represented approximately 0.5% of the customer
base but generated more than 70% of corporate revenue.
(viii) The Sports Betting and Related Interactive
Gambling in Pennsylvania Study reported that certain
promotions advertised as "free bets" or similar
incentives may require consumers to wager extraordinary
sums before becoming eligible to receive or withdraw the
advertised benefit, creating a substantial risk that
consumers may be misled regarding the nature and value of
the promotions. The study cited one example in which a

(15) The Sports Betting and Related Interactive Gambling
in Pennsylvania Study recommended or identified for
legislative consideration the following:
(i) Adopting a public health approach to the
regulation of sports betting and related interactive
gambling that emphasizes prevention, early intervention,
harm reduction, evidence-based policymaking and the
protection of public health and safety.
(ii) Requiring the collection and analysis of
anonymized player data to improve understanding of how
gambling addiction develops and progresses, distinguish
gambling products and practices that are associated with
greater and lesser levels of gambling-related harm,
develop evidence-based harm-minimization strategies and
create systems to monitor, detect and intervene in high-
risk gambling.
(iii) Prohibiting the direct or indirect use of
credit cards to fund online gambling accounts.
(iv) Requiring registered players to establish
limits relating to gambling losses, the continuous
duration of play and the number of deposits made within a
specified period of time.
(v) Strengthening protections against gambling
advertisements and promotions directed toward or
disproportionately viewed by minors and young adults.
(vi) Restricting direct gambling promotions sent to
individuals who are not actively logged into an online
gambling platform.

(16) The United States Congress has initiated multiple

Several states have enacted laws and regulations to increase

§ 6003. Definitions.
The following words and phrases when used in this chapter
shall have the meanings given to them in this section unless the
context clearly indicates otherwise:
"Board." The Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board.
"Department." The Department of Drug and Alcohol Programs of
the Commonwealth.
"Fund." The Compulsive and Problem Gambling Treatment Fund
established under 4 Pa.C.S. § 1509 (relating to c ompulsive and
problem gambling program) .
"Gross interactive gaming revenue." As defined in 4 Pa.C.S.
§ 1103 (relating to definitions).
"Gross interactive sports wagering revenue." As follows:
(1) The total of cash or cash equivalents received from
interactive sports wagering minus the total of:
(i) Cash or cash equivalents paid to players as a
result of interactive sports wagering.
(ii) Cash or cash equivalents paid to purchase
annuities to fund prizes payable to players over a period
of time as a result of interactive sports wagering.
(iii) The actual cost paid by the sports wagering

(2) The term does not include any of the following:
(i) Counterfeit cash.
(ii) Coins or currency of other countries received

holder to record the balance of a registered player's debits,

"Microbet." A proposition bet on a sporting event that is
wagered live while the sporting event is ongoing and concerns
the outcome of a play or action occurring in the sporting event.
"Online gambling." A type of wagering licensed by the board
that includes interactive gaming and interactive sports
wagering.
"Online gambling platform." An interactive gaming device,
interactive gaming platform, interactive gaming website, sports
wagering device or other technology approved by the board for
use in relation to the conduct of online gambling by an
interactive gaming certificate holder, interactive gaming
operator, sports wagering certificate holder or sports wagering
operator to conduct online gambling.
"Proposition bet." A sports wager on the individual
performance statistics of athletes participating in a sporting
event, or combination of sporting events, placed on the
occurrence or nonoccurrence of a specific act, statistic,
performance, event or circumstance within a sporting event or
series of sporting events, including bets on individual player
performance, officiating decisions, penalties, injuries, timing
of events or any outcome other than the final result or score of
a sporting event. The term includes pre-sporting event and in-
sporting event bets.

§ 6005. Online gambling public health protections.
An interactive gaming certificate holder, interactive gaming
operator, sports wagering certificate holder, sports wagering
operator or any affiliate, intermediary, subsidiary or holding
company of such an entity may not directly or indirectly engage
in any of the following acts in conjunction with the conduct of
online gambling:
(1) Accept more than two separate deposits from or on
behalf of an individual during a 24-hour period.
(2) Accept deposits through the Internet or another form
of electronic payment that, singularly or in the aggregate,
exceed $5,000 during any 180-day period, unless the
interactive gaming certificate holder, interactive gaming
operator, sports wagering certificate holder or sports
wagering operator has verified the individual's affordability
under paragraph (3).
(3) Accept deposits in excess of $5,000 during any 180-
day period from or on behalf of an individual without
completing an affordability assessment in accordance with
criteria established by the department under section 6004(a)
(4) (relating to duties of department, Online Problem
Gambling Public Health Task Force and cooperation). The
affordability assessment:
(i) May include:
(A) Consumer-authorized verification of income
or financial assets through a secure third-party
financial data provider.
(B) Review of documentation voluntarily
submitted by the individual.

(ii) Shall reasonably determine that the proposed

is inconsistent with the department's criteria shall be
rejected and not accepted by the interactive gaming

Any financial information collected for the affordability

(4) Other than an initial wager placed after a
registered player has established an interactive gaming
account or an interactive sports wagering account, accept a
wager by an individual within 15 minutes of the making of a

(5) Accept a wager in excess of $2 per play of an
interactive game from an individual between 21 and 25 years

(6) Accept a wager in excess of $5 per play of an
interactive game from an individual over 25 years of age.
(7) Accept a wager from an individual between 21 and 25
years of age if the individual has aggregate losses totaling
$750 or more in a 24-hour period or at least $2,500 in a 30-
day period. In the event total losses meet or exceed the 24-
hour limit, wagers may not be accepted from the individual

§ 6007. Problem gambling education, prevention, treatment and
funding.
(a) Assessment authorized.--To further the department's
implementation and administration of this chapter, an assessment
in the amount equal to 0.0075 multiplied by the total gross
interactive gaming revenue and the total gross interactive
sports wagering revenue shall be paid by each active or
operating interactive gaming certificate holder, or an
interactive gaming operator on its behalf, and sports wagering
certificate holder, or sports wagering operator on its behalf.
(b) Collection and deposit.--The assessment established in
this section shall be collected by the Department of Revenue and
deposited into a restricted account established in the fund.
(c) Use of assessment.--
(1) The money in the restricted account is appropriated
on a continuing basis to the department for the purpose of
problem-gambling education, prevention, treatment and
research and the establishment and maintenance of research
data infrastructure, all as related to online gambling. The
research may include monitoring and evaluating the public
health impacts of online gambling and the effectiveness of
this chapter and developing and evaluating evidence-based

(2) The department shall have exclusive authority to

(3) Neither the board nor any interactive gaming

affiliate, intermediary, subsidiary or holding company
thereof shall direct, control, approve or otherwise influence
the allocation or expenditure of money deposited into the
restricted account.
§ 6008. Data collection for research.
(a) Research authorized.--For the purpose of research only,
a public institution of higher education in this Commonwealth or
qualified research organizations specializing in addiction
related research or treatment shall be permitted to analyze
transaction-level data and metrics related to online gambling
operations conducted in this Commonwealth.
(b) Access to data.--
(1) Upon the request of a public institution of higher
education in this Commonwealth or qualified research
organization specializing in addiction-related research or
treatment, each interactive gaming certificate holder,
interactive gaming operator, sports wagering certificate
holder and sports wagering operator shall provide
transaction-level data and metrics in a timely manner and no
less frequently than quarterly.
(2) A public institution of higher education in this
Commonwealth or qualified research organization specializing

(4) A public institution of higher education in this

§ 6009. Rulemaking.
The department may adopt necessary rules and regulations for
the implementation and administration of this chapter, and the
department may consult with the board, which shall cooperate
with the department with regard to such rules and regulations.

§ 6010. Enforcement.
(a) Office of Enforcement Counsel.--This chapter may be
enforced by the Office of Enforcement Counsel and Bureau of
Investigation and Enforcement of the board, which has the
authority and power specified in 4 Pa.C.S. Pt. II (relating to
gaming). The provisions of 4 Pa.C.S. § 1518(c), (d) and (e)
(relating to prohibited acts; penalties) shall apply to conduct
in violation of this chapter.
(b) Relation to other laws.--A violation of this chapter is
a violation of the act of December 17, 1968 (P.L.1224, No.387),
known as the Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law.
§ 6011. Severability.
The provisions of this chapter are severable. If any
provision of this chapter or its application to any person or
circumstances is held invalid, the invalidity shall not affect
other provisions or applications of this chapter which can be
given effect without the invalid provision or application.
Section 2. This act shall take effect in 60 days.
